d: The outer, multinucleated layer of the placental villi that faces maternal blood. It secretes hCG, human placental lactogen, progesterone and estrogen.
The handover of progesterone production from the corpus luteum, kept alive by hCG, to the placenta at about 7 to 10 weeks of gestation.
A syncytiotrophoblast hormone, also called chorionic somatomammotropin, that rises with placental mass. It causes maternal insulin resistance and lipolysis, which spares glucose for the fetus.
Dizziness and low blood pressure when a woman past about 20 weeks lies flat, because the uterus compresses the inferior vena cava and cuts venous return. Lying on her left side relieves it.
The physiologic fall in hemoglobin concentration in pregnancy, because plasma volume expands by 40 to 50 percent while red cell mass rises only 20 to 30 percent.
The volume left in the lungs after a normal breath out. It falls about 20 percent in pregnancy because the uterus pushes the diaphragm up.
A peptide hormone from the corpus luteum and placenta that loosens the pubic symphysis and pelvic ligaments and adds to the vasodilation of pregnancy.
The liver protein that carries most circulating T4. Estrogen raises it in pregnancy, so total T4 rises while free T4 and TSH stay normal.
The progesterone-driven change of endometrial stromal cells into glycogen- and lipid-rich decidual cells that feed the embryo and limit trophoblast invasion.

Pressure of the pregnant uterus on the inferior vena cava and aorta when she lies on her back after about 20 weeks. It lowers venous return, cardiac output and uterine blood flow, and a left lateral tilt relieves it.
